papers.title: A droplet-based long-read single-cell epigenome sequencing method for the high-throughput profiling of multidimensional regulatory elements within individual cells.
papers.abstract: Recently, long-read sequencing methods have revolutionized genomic research by allowing the resolution of previously inaccessible regions across the genome. However, the throughput and scalability of these methods have hindered their general application in the field. To address this limitation, we developed droplet-based methods for the single-cell profiling of chromatin accessibility (droplet-based single-cell Nanopore ATAC-seq, dscNanoATAC) and histone modifications (droplet-based single-cell NanoCUT&Tag, dscNanoCUT) by combining a commercial microfluidic device and long-read sequencing plat
papers.summary: The authors developed droplet-based long-read single-cell epigenome sequencing methods, dscNanoATAC and dscNanoCUT, that combine a commercial microfluidic device with nanopore sequencing to profile chromatin accessibility and histone modifications in individual cells at high throughput. This addresses the scalability bottleneck of prior long-read single-cell epigenomics, enabling multidimensional regulatory element profiling per cell.

papers.title: CDState Resolves Malignant Cell Heterogeneity from Bulk Tumor RNA Sequencing Data.
papers.abstract: Intratumor transcriptional heterogeneity (ITTH), defined as the coexistence of diverse cell states within a single tumor, complicates cancer treatment and contributes to variable therapeutic responses. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) can resolve this complexity, its cost and technical demands limit large-scale use. Bulk RNA-seq provides a scalable alternative but requires computational methods to deconvolve bulk transcriptomes into distinct cell states. Existing supervised approaches rely on accurate reference data, which are lacking for many cancer types, whereas unsupervised
papers.summary: CDState is a computational method that deconvolves bulk tumor RNA sequencing data to resolve intratumor transcriptional heterogeneity into distinct malignant cell states without requiring supervised reference data. This enables scalable profiling of cell-state diversity across large cancer cohorts where single-cell sequencing is impractical.

papers.title: CQRM: A Composite Quantile Regression Model for Differential Expression Analysis of Non-Coding RNA Count Data.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) play important roles in various biological processes, primarily via regulating gene expression at multiple levels. Nevertheless, compared to protein-coding genes, ncRNAs are relatively understudied. They are characterized by low expression, large variation, and more dynamic expression across different tissues and cell types, which creates unique challenges in differential expression (DE) analysis. Methods: We propose the CQRM, an adaptive multi-quantile testing framework for ncRNA count data that incorporates jittering to accommodate discrete cou
papers.summary: The authors propose CQRM, a composite quantile regression framework for differential expression analysis of non-coding RNA count data. It uses adaptive multi-quantile testing with jittering to handle the discrete, low-expression, and highly variable nature of ncRNA counts. This addresses limitations of standard DE methods that assume higher expression levels and less variability.

papers.title: The gene expression signature of multinucleated giant cells in the spleens of Leishmania donovani-infected mice.
papers.abstract: Multinucleated giant cells (MGCs) are associated with chronic inflammation and infectious diseases, but their biological characteristics in vivo remain poorly understood because intact cells are difficult to isolate from tissues. In visceral leishmaniasis, heavily parasitized, hemophagocytic MGCs are observed in the spleens of Leishmania donovani-infected mice, suggesting that these cells may contribute to parasite persistence and disease pathology. In this study, we established a method for isolating intact MGCs from the spleens of chronically infected BALB/c mice and performed transcriptomic
papers.summary: The authors developed a method to isolate intact multinucleated giant cells (MGCs) from the spleens of mice chronically infected with Leishmania donovani, overcoming the difficulty of recovering these cells from tissue. Transcriptomic profiling of these MGCs reveals a gene expression signature that may explain their role in parasite persistence and disease pathology in visceral leishmaniasis.

papers.title: Integrative bulk and single-cell transcriptomics identifies a HERC5-linked immune-attenuated risk program for pulmonary metastasis/relapse in osteosarcoma.
papers.abstract: Pulmonary metastasis/relapse (PM/R) is a major cause of osteosarcoma treatment failure. We aimed to develop a compact transcriptomic PM/R risk score and characterize associated immune and single-cell programs.
papers.summary: This study integrates bulk and single-cell transcriptomic data to build a compact risk score predicting pulmonary metastasis/relapse in osteosarcoma, identifying a HERC5-linked immune-attenuated program associated with poor outcomes. The work links a specific gene signature to immune suppression and single-cell-level programs, offering a potential prognostic tool for this aggressive cancer.

papers.title: NoiBic: a noise-tolerant biclustering algorithm for high-throughput gene expression data analysis.
papers.abstract: High-throughput transcriptomic technologies generate large-scale gene expression datasets for functional module discovery. However, technical and biological noise can obscure coherent expression patterns and compromise module detection. Noise-tolerant methods are therefore needed to recover meaningful biclusters.
papers.summary: NoiBic is a new biclustering algorithm designed to tolerate noise in high-throughput gene expression data, aiming to recover coherent gene-sample modules that noise would otherwise obscure. The work addresses a common challenge in transcriptomic analysis where technical and biological variability degrades module detection, and provides a noise-tolerant approach for functional module discovery.

papers.title: PRISM-GEP: Viewing single-cell expression through the lens of topic modeling.
papers.abstract: Gene-expression programs (GEPs) are the co-regulated gene modules whose coordinated activity encodes biological processes. Recovering them from single-cell RNA-seq is hard because regulation is many-to-many. A cell can run several programs at once, and a gene can take part in several. Methods that resolve programs along a trajectory break this structure by assigning each gene to a single program.
papers.summary: PRISM-GEP is a new computational method that uses topic modeling to identify gene-expression programs (co-regulated gene modules) from single-cell RNA-seq data. Unlike trajectory-based approaches that force each gene into a single program, it allows genes to participate in multiple programs and cells to run several programs simultaneously, better reflecting the many-to-many nature of gene regulation.

papers.title: Computational deconvolution of drug sensitivity via single-cell-to-bulk transcriptome mapping.
papers.abstract: Analyses routinely conducted in both fundamental research and biomedical studies often report aggregate signals derived from heterogeneous mixtures of cells. These mixtures reflect the intrinsic anatomical and functional complexity of the tissues and organs from which they are derived. Such bulk measurements obscure cell-specific signals, thereby hindering accurate interpretation of the underlying biological processes. Here, we introduce CLIMB and CLIFF, a two-step machine-learning framework that deconvolves bulk RNA-seq into cell-type composition and expression, and then resolves bulk drug se
papers.summary: CLIMB and CLIFF form a two-step machine-learning framework that deconvolves bulk RNA-seq into cell-type composition and cell-type-specific expression, then maps these to drug sensitivity. This enables drug-response prediction from heterogeneous bulk samples by resolving cell-specific signals that would otherwise be obscured.

papers.title: Single-Cell and Bulk RNA-Seq Profiling Identifies Cell Adhesion-Related Gene Signatures in Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury.
papers.abstract: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) involves complex secondary damage mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and blood-brain barrier disruption, in which cell adhesion-related genes (CARGs) play a central role. Therefore, systematically elucidating the expression and regulation of CARGs is crucial for identifying new therapeutic targets to mitigate inflammatory infiltration and preserve barrier integrity. Both single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. The single-cell data were processed using Seurat, and CARG activi
papers.summary: This study integrates single-cell and bulk RNA-seq data from public repositories to characterize cell adhesion-related gene expression patterns in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury. The authors identify cell adhesion gene signatures that may serve as therapeutic targets for reducing inflammatory infiltration and preserving blood-brain barrier integrity after stroke.

papers.title: Integrative single-cell sequencing and machine learning analyses identify chronic inflammation and cancer-associated fibroblast subsets as drivers of adverse outcomes in ovarian cancer.
papers.abstract: Ovarian cancer remains the deadliest gynecological malignancy, with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) often leaving residual fibroblast-enriched disease.
papers.summary: This study integrates single-cell sequencing data with machine learning to characterize the ovarian cancer microenvironment, identifying chronic inflammation and specific cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) subsets as key drivers of poor clinical outcomes. The findings highlight how residual fibroblast-enriched disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy contributes to adverse prognosis, suggesting potential targets for improved therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Pasta, a Versatile Transcriptomic Clock, Maps the Chemical and Genetic Determinants of Aging and Rejuvenation.
papers.abstract: With the growing burden of age-related diseases, understanding and modulating the aging process has become a priority. Transcriptomic aging clocks (TACs) can track biological age but remain limited by platform dependence, tissue specificity, or restricted accessibility. To address this, we developed Pasta, a robust and broadly applicable human TAC, built using a novel 'age-shift' learning framework. Pasta accurately predicted relative age across diverse tissues and data types, including bulk and single-cell RNA-Seq as well as microarray data. Its predictions aligned with senescent and stem-lik
papers.summary: The authors present Pasta, a transcriptomic aging clock trained with a novel 'age-shift' learning framework that predicts relative biological age across diverse tissues and data types, including bulk and single-cell RNA-seq and microarray data. The clock's predictions align with senescence and stem-like states, and it was used to map chemical and genetic determinants of aging and rejuvenation. This provides a versatile, platform-independent tool for studying aging biology.

papers.title: Spatial biology in cancer epigenetics.
papers.abstract: Cancer develops inside organized tissue environments wherein cellular behavior is heavily influenced by local interactions and spatially restricted regulatory programs. While bulk and single-cell sequencing technologies have fundamentally revolutionized our understanding of tumor biology, these techniques often disrupt tissue architecture and therefore fail to capture the spatial context in which molecular processes occur. Spatial transcriptomics has provided important insights into tumor heterogeneity, microenvironmental organization, and cell-to-cell communication. However, gene expression a
papers.summary: This review discusses how spatial biology approaches, particularly spatial transcriptomics, can be applied to cancer epigenetics to study how local tissue context shapes regulatory programs in tumors. It argues that while bulk and single-cell sequencing have advanced tumor biology, they lose spatial information, and that integrating spatial methods with epigenetic analysis is needed to understand tumor heterogeneity, microenvironment organization, and cell-cell communication.

papers.title: A unified developmental timeline of pigmented ocular tissues in the mouse eye.
papers.abstract: Pigmented tissues of the vertebrate eye are essential for optical performance, metabolic support, and tissue homeostasis, yet their coordinated development has been difficult to study because melanin interferes with histological and immunohistochemical analyses. Here, we apply a gentle hydrogen peroxide based bleaching method compatible with IHC for Rpe65, Rhodopsin, ZO-1, Cralbp/Rlbp1, S100b, and Cd34, and examined Dct/Tyrp2 expression, to generate a unified developmental atlas of all pigmented tissues in the mouse eye. We also re-analyzed published single-cell RNA-seq datasets from developin
papers.summary: The authors developed a gentle hydrogen peroxide bleaching method that removes melanin pigment while preserving tissue for immunohistochemistry, enabling them to map the development of all pigmented tissues in the mouse eye on a unified timeline. They combined this with markers for retinal pigment epithelium, neural retina, and vasculature, plus reanalysis of published single-cell RNA-seq data, to create a developmental atlas of pigmented ocular tissues.

papers.title: Condition-Associated Pattern Extraction and Recovery From Multi-Condition Single-Cell RNA-seq Data With CAPER.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in multi-condition single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data analysis is the disentanglement of true biological signals from unwanted variations in complex experimental designs. Current statistical and machine learning-based methods struggle with this task, often providing only visualizable embeddings, over-correcting and discarding biological signal, or failing to resolve cell-type-specific responses. Here, we present CAPER, a matrix factorization framework that explicitly disentangles shared biological states from condition-specific variations. CAPER directly outputs an
papers.summary: CAPER is a matrix factorization framework for multi-condition scRNA-seq that explicitly separates shared biological states from condition-specific variation, rather than producing only visual embeddings or over-correcting away real signal. It outputs interpretable condition-associated patterns and can recover them, addressing cell-type-specific responses that existing statistical and machine-learning methods often fail to resolve.

papers.title: Normalization choice drives biological interpretation in single-cell RNA-seq cancer studies: A systematic benchmarking of 465 computational pipelines.
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has transformed our understanding of tumor heterogeneity, yet the impact of computational pipeline choices on biological conclusions remains poorly characterized. Here, we systematically benchmark 465 combinations of 5 normalization methods and 4 clustering algorithms across 3 cancer datasets encompassing over 434,000 cells. We introduce the Biological Discordance Score (BDS), a metric that quantifies how marker gene interpretation changes across pipelines. We find that normalization method choice has a greater impact on biological interpretation than clu
papers.summary: This study benchmarks 465 computational pipelines (combinations of normalization methods and clustering algorithms) across three cancer scRNA-seq datasets totaling over 434,000 cells. The authors introduce a Biological Discordance Score to quantify how marker gene interpretation shifts across pipelines, and find that normalization choice affects biological interpretation more than clustering algorithm choice. The work highlights that computational pipeline decisions can materially change conclusions drawn from single-cell cancer studies.

papers.title: Molecular traces of microbial cross-kingdom migration: from the gut ecosystem to the intervertebral disc microenvironment.
papers.abstract: Low back pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide, and lumbar intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) is strongly associated with its development. Recent studies have shown that the gut microbiota (GM) and its metabolites may be involved in the occurrence and development of IVDD through the gut-disc axis. However, the key microbes mediating this process and their specific molecular mechanisms remain unclear.
papers.journal: The spine journal : official journal of the North American Spine Society
papers.summary: This study investigates the 'gut-disc axis' hypothesis, proposing that gut microbes and their metabolites migrate to intervertebral discs and contribute to disc degeneration (IVDD), a major cause of low back pain. The authors aim to identify the key microbial species involved and the molecular mechanisms by which they influence the disc microenvironment, though the abstract does not report specific findings.

papers.title: Integrative single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analysis identifies monocyte/macrophage senescence-associated candidate genes in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
papers.abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vascular disorder characterized by immune dysregulation and vascular remodeling. Cellular senescence modulates immune responses, but its role in PAH, particularly in monocytes/macrophages, remains unclear. Here, we integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data to identify senescence-associated candidate genes associated with monocytes/macrophages in PAH.
papers.summary: This study integrates single-cell and bulk transcriptomic datasets to identify senescence-associated genes specifically in monocytes/macrophages in pulmonary arterial hypertension. The authors propose candidate genes linking immune cell senescence to PAH vascular remodeling, though the findings are computational and require experimental validation.

papers.title: Patient classification using single-cell RNA-sequencing data with deep learning convolutional neural networks.
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables gene expression profiling at the resolution of individual cells, revealing cellular heterogeneity that is obscured in bulk RNA-seq. While this offers a powerful lens to study disease-specific changes, leveraging scRNA-seq data for patient phenotype classification remains challenging due to limited sample numbers, cell count variability, high dimensionality, and dependence on cell-type annotations. Existing tools attempt to address these issues using probabilistic models or attention mechanisms, but face limitations in scalability, interpretability
papers.summary: The paper presents a deep learning convolutional neural network approach for classifying patient phenotypes directly from single-cell RNA-sequencing data, aiming to overcome challenges such as limited sample sizes, variable cell counts, and high dimensionality. It addresses limitations of existing probabilistic and attention-based tools, particularly around scalability and interpretability, though the abstract does not report specific performance results.

papers.title: FDX1 is associated with CALR abundance and JAK-STAT-related inflammatory signaling in myeloproliferative neoplasms.
papers.abstract: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are driven by constitutive cytokine-receptor signaling, yet the metabolic programs associated with driver genotype and inflammatory remodeling remain incompletely defined.
papers.summary: This study investigates the metabolic protein FDX1 in myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), finding that its expression is associated with the abundance of CALR (a key MPN driver gene) and with JAK-STAT-related inflammatory signaling. The work links a metabolic factor to genotype-specific inflammatory remodeling in MPNs, suggesting FDX1 as a potential node connecting metabolism and cytokine signaling.
